figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Human-to-robot task transfer with H2RB. H2RB transfers task experience from human videos to robots using pretrained VLAs by bridging the cross-embodiment perception and action gaps, without target-robot demonstrations or paired demonstrations.
figures.headline: H2RB transfers task experience from human videos to robots without target-robot or paired demonstrations.
citing_sentences: Together, these components enable human-to-robot task transfer while facilitating learning from heterogeneous human-robot experience, as illustrated in Figure 1.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Overview of H2RB. (a) A shared temporal encoder maps human and robot action chunks into a common latent action space, while embodiment-specific decoders reconstruct actions for each domain. (b) Hand geometry-anchored alignment grounds VLA conditioning across embodiments, while the frozen encoder provides latent action targets.
figures.headline: Latent action targets come from a frozen encoder, while hand-geometry alignment grounds conditioning features across embodiments.
citing_sentences: H2RB bridges human-robot gaps through shared latent actions with embodiment-specific decoders and geometry-grounded VLM features, as illustrated in Figure 2.

Specifically, given human actions $\mathbf{A}^{H}_{t}$ and robot actions $\mathbf{A}^{R}_{t}$ in a common wrist-hand representation, we train a variational action autoencoder (Kingma and Welling, 2013) with a shared encoder and embodiment-specific decoders (see Figure 2(a)).
Aligning actions alone does not resolve the human-robot perceptual gap, so we anchor VLM conditioning features to hand geometry shared across embodiments (Figure 2(b)).

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Qualitative human-to-robot transfer rollouts. (a) H2RB is trained jointly on human and robot demonstrations. (b) The trained policy executes target tasks introduced through human demonstrations, including object transfer on box, followed by skill transfer on opening.
figures.headline: Rollouts show the trained policy performing a box object transfer followed by an opening skill absent from robot demonstrations.
citing_sentences: Skill transfer introduces opening and closing interactions absent from the source robot demonstrations (see Figure 3).

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: RB-Y1 parcel-handling task. Box flipping (top) and polybag handling (bottom).
figures.headline: The parcel task requires flipping boxes and polybags to expose their shipping labels before pushing them onward.
citing_sentences: For heterogeneous training evaluation, we additionally consider an RB-Y1 parcel-handling task, where the robot flips boxes and polybags to expose their shipping labels before pushing them onward (see Figure 4).

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Human-robot HT. Human-robot HT and geometry grounding improves robot-only downstream success.
figures.headline: Heterogeneous training and geometry grounding raise robot-only parcel-handling success from 64% to 72% to 78%.
citing_sentences: For RB-Y1, parcel-orientation success improves from 64% with robot-only training to 72% with human-robot HT and 78% with geometry-grounded HT, as shown in Figure 5.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Effect of human-robot HT. HT improves transfer abilities, showing the scalability of H2RB.
figures.headline: Heterogeneous training raises OpenArm object transfer from 51.8 to 57.2 and skill transfer from 62.7 to 81.7.
citing_sentences: For OpenArm, heterogeneous training improves object transfer from 51.8 to 57.2 (+5.4) and skill transfer from 62.7 to 81.7 (+19.0), as shown in Figure 6.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Instruction conditioning. Instruction conditioning improves skill transfer abilities.
figures.headline: Instruction conditioning raises skill transfer from 62.7 to 83.3.
citing_sentences: As shown in Figure 7, this improves skill transfer from 62.7 to 83.3 (+20.6), suggesting that sustained instruction access helps preserve task semantics during cross-embodiment execution.

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Failure case analysis of human-to-robot transfer. (a) Fails to complete the grasp. (b) Unrelated to the target object location. (c) Fails to produce a hand pose suitable for grasping. (d) Executes a robot-observed pick-and-place motion in human-observed task environment.
figures.headline: Failure cases include an incomplete grasp, a misdirected reach, an invalid grasp pose, and a robot pick-and-place instead of opening.
citing_sentences: Human-only policies capture the demonstrated interaction pattern but fail near contact due to inaccurate wrist alignment and grasp configuration (Figure 8(a)), whereas robot-only policies produce executable robot motions but fail to localize or reproduce behaviors absent from robot demonstrations (Figure 8(b)).
The shared-action baseline produces invalid grasp poses, indicating that coordinate-level alignment does not resolve the remaining perceptual mismatch (Figure 8(c)).

Moreover, robot-conditioned predictions can remain closer to the robot latent distribution and revert to familiar robot behaviors even in human task deployment, such as pick-and-place instead of the human-demonstrated opening motion (Figure 8(d)).

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: PCA visualization of cross-embodiment representation adaptation. (a) Vision-language conditioning features with hand geometry-anchored alignment alone (left) and H2RB (right). Arrows show adapter-induced displacements for the same observation. (b) Action-tokenizer latents without (left) and with (right) cross-domain latent regression, using per-tokenizer PCA. Human I and II denote human tasks trained in within-skill object transfer and skill transfer, respectively.
figures.headline: H2RB shifts robot conditioning features toward the human distribution, and cross-domain regression brings latent distributions closer.
citing_sentences: Compared with the Ego-Pi-shared action baseline, the PCA projection in Figure 9(a) shows that H2RB shifts robot conditioning features toward the human distribution, reducing the human-robot gap.

The two-dimensional projections in Figure 9(b) provide a qualitative view of this alignment, showing how cross-domain regression brings the human and robot latent distributions closer in the action latent space.

(b) For object transfer, in-distribution (ID) rollouts are sampled from four workspace quadrants (right-upper, right-lower, left-upper, and left-lower), with five rollouts per quadrant and randomized object orientation. Out-of-distribution (OOD) rollouts are sampled outside the ID placement region (red area), again with randomized orientation. For skill transfer, the initial openness of the air fryer is randomized for all 30 trials.
figures.headline: OpenArm evaluation uses four in-distribution workspace quadrants and an out-of-distribution area outside the placement region.
citing_sentences: Figure 10 illustrates the corresponding ID and OOD placement regions.

figures.caption: Qualitative transferred-task rollouts. Representative successful H2RB executions on box, ball, towel, open, and close, spanning both object-level and skill-level transfer.
figures.headline: Representative successful rollouts cover box, ball, towel, open, and close transfer tasks.
citing_sentences: Representative successful rollouts for each transfer task are shown in Figure 11.

figures.caption: RB-Y1 experimental setup. (a) Bimanual robot platform. (b) Boxes and polybags used for parcel handling.
figures.headline: The bimanual robot platform and the boxes and polybags used for parcel handling are shown.
citing_sentences: We evaluate robot-only adaptation on the RB-Y1 bimanual platform, equipped with two 7-DoF arms and two 20-DoF Wuji Hand 2 dexterous hands, as shown in Figure 12(a).
The task requires orienting parcels (Figure 12(b)), including boxes and polybags, such that their shipping labels face upward, and transferring them onto a conveyor belt.

abstract: Pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies provide a strong starting point for deployment, but adapting them to a target robot and environment still requires costly embodiment-specific demonstrations. Human demonstrations are far easier to collect, yet directly leveraging them is challenging due to the substantial human-robot embodiment gap, particularly when the underlying VLA has been pretrained primarily on robot data. We introduce H2RB (Human-To-Robot Bridge), a human-robot co-training framework for adapting pretrained VLA policies from unpaired human and robot demonstrations. H2RB bridges the embodiment gap at both interfaces: geometry-anchored alignment grounds human and robot observations in a compatible representation, while a decoupled-decoder tokenizer shares action latents without forcing both domains through a single action mapping. This design allows human demonstrations to provide useful behavioral supervision while retaining the rich visual, semantic, and control priors of the pretrained VLA. Across real-world tasks, H2RB substantially improves object transfer performance from 8.0 to 51.8 and enables skill transfer to score 62.7, in settings where co-train baselines totally fail to transfer human-demonstrated skills. The benefit also persists under object-placement shifts, improving out-of-distribution transfer from 6.0 to 45.3. H2RB suggests a way for human demonstrations to serve as a scalable supervision source for adapting pretrained robotic policies, reducing the dependence on costly target-robot data collection.

sections.body: The paper states that collecting target-robot demonstrations needs physical access, teleoperation, and repeated environment resets, while human demonstrations can be collected with a lightweight camera setup. Prior methods place human and robot data in a shared action space but leave perceptual differences unresolved. H2RB adds geometry-anchored alignment of vision-language features and a decoupled-decoder latent tokenizer. On OpenArm, object transfer rises from 8.0 to 51.8, and skill transfer reaches 62.7, where shared-action co-training baselines fail. On RB-Y1, robot-only adaptation success improves from 72% to 78% under matched heterogeneous training.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Target-robot demonstrations are costly, so the paper proposes adapting pretrained robot policies using human demonstrations.

sections.body:
H2RB converts human and robot actions into a shared wrist-hand format covering wrist position, a 6D wrist rotation, and hand joint angles. A variational action autoencoder with one shared encoder and embodiment-specific decoders produces frozen latent action targets for a flow-matching policy. A residual adapter and a training-only readout predict the current hand geometry from pooled conditioning tokens. The training objective adds this geometry loss to the prediction loss:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{VLA}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pred}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{geo}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{geo}}
$$

Because each observation supplies its own geometry target, the alignment needs no paired human-robot demonstrations or temporal correspondence. At deployment, the human decoder converts predicted latents into robot commands.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: H2RB pairs a shared latent action tokenizer with separate decoders and grounds vision-language features in hand geometry.

sections.body: Experiments use an OpenArm humanoid with Inspire hands, with policies initialized from the robot-pretrained RLDX-1-IMG. Scores are weighted task scores from 0 to 100. On object transfer, vanilla co-training reaches 8.0, while H2RB reaches 51.8 (+43.8). Under placement shift, H2RB improves over Ego-Pi-shared action from 21.3 to 45.3 out of distribution. On skill transfer, Ego-Pi-shared action scores 0.0 for both Open and Close, while H2RB reaches 50.7 and 74.7. Heterogeneous training raises OpenArm scores to 57.2 and 81.7, and instruction conditioning raises skill transfer to 83.3. The RB-Y1 parcel task uses binary success over 50 trials.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: H2RB scores 62.7 on skill transfer where shared-action co-training baselines score 0.0 on both skills.

sections.body: Human-only policies fail near contact because of inaccurate wrist alignment, while robot-only policies fail to reproduce behaviors absent from robot data. In the ablation in Table 3(a), adding the action tokenizer raises object transfer from 34.7 to 43.3 and enables skill transfer from 0.0 to 49.7. Cross-domain latent regression reduces the normalized human-robot latent gap from 3.81 to 1.53, a 59.8% reduction, and reaches 51.8 and 62.7. Policies trained from human demonstrations move at 7.36 cm/s, compared with 2.52 cm/s for a robot-only policy, with scores of 62.7 and 65.3. The section attributes the retained speed to the embodiment-specific decoders.
sections.heading: Analysis
sections.headline: Latent alignment reduces the human-robot latent gap from 3.81 to 1.53 and preserves faster human-demonstrated motion.

sections.body: The section groups related work into three areas. Human-video methods use reconstructed hand motion or latent actions inferred from frame transitions. Cross-embodiment alignment methods use paired demonstrations, trajectory-based pseudo-pairs, or synthesized robot-domain observations. Latent action methods use embodiment-specific decoders for heterogeneous end-effectors. The authors position H2RB as grounding pretrained VLA features in hand geometry for each observation, without paired data, trajectory matching, image synthesis, or a prior human-robot backbone training stage.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior alignment methods rely on paired demonstrations, trajectory pseudo-pairs, or synthesized robot-domain images.

sections.body: The conclusion describes H2RB as a framework for adapting pretrained VLAs from unpaired human and robot demonstrations. It bridges perception through hand geometry-anchored alignment and action through a shared latent space with embodiment-specific decoders. The section reports improved object and skill transfer on OpenArm, further gains from heterogeneous training, and benefits for robot-only adaptation on a different embodiment. The authors state that the findings concern reusable action-relevant structure learned without enforcing identical action dynamics.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: H2RB improves human-to-robot transfer and robot-only adaptation, with further gains from heterogeneous training.

sections.body: The appendix gives action and geometry dimensions, the tokenizer architecture, the reconstruction, KL, centroid, and covariance terms, and the geometry and flow-matching objectives. Table 14 lists 14,548 episodes and 5,014,530 frames across five heterogeneous sources. The tokenizers are trained from scratch for 100k steps. Robot-only fine-tuning for the parcel-handling task uses 726,752 frames and 30k updates, with success scored as binary over 50 trials.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists implementation details, tokenizer and loss definitions, heterogeneous training data, and a parcel-handling evaluation protocol.
